own_solution.law: Steady radial Fourier conduction gives ΔT(r)=(Tin−Tout)ln(r/r1)/ln(r2/r1). Thus ΔT(5 cm)=120 ln(5/3)/ln(9/3)=55.7968 K. Adding thickness q changes the denominator to ln((9+q)/3), with q in centimetres.
assumptions: The insulation is homogeneous, has constant thermal conductivity and has no internal heat generation.
Heat conduction is steady and purely radial.
When further insulation is added to the pipe, the prescribed 300 K temperature applies to the new outermost surface.

notes: The authors' claims agree with the locked pass-1 review. Added pipe insulation of 1.2, 1.8 and 2.5 cm gives falls of 50.0901, 47.8550 and 45.6184 K, respectively. Conductivity cancels for all listed positive values because both surface temperatures are prescribed. Earlier-survey insulation is explicitly restricted to that earlier event; tank insulation does not change the pipe's prescribed boundaries. The stated numerical minimal pairs preserve 1.8 cm and change only the relevant object or event attachment. The two numeral-free controls correctly replace that measurement with 'small thickness' and are explicitly identified as controls. Logarithm arguments are dimensionless; centimetres are sufficient for radius ratios, while SI radii give heat current per unit length in W/m. All certified answers have adequate precision.
